content.caveat: Popular descriptions such as “random-looking” or “small errors grow” are not by themselves mathematical definitions of chaos.
content.exact: QEVA Protocol 0.1 assigns no universal predicate Chaos(T). A record claiming chaos must identify a contextual criterion (for example a named topological, measure-theoretic, symbolic, or metric definition) and state its hypotheses.
content.example: A map may satisfy sensitive dependence while failing some stronger named chaos criterion.
content.plain: “Chaos” has several rigorous definitions. QEVA should name the definition being used instead of treating the word as self-explanatory.

assumptions.text: A group G acts on X.
H is an index-2 subgroup of orientation-preserving transformations.
r is any element of G\H.

content.caveat: Chirality is relative to a declared transformation group and an orientation-preserving subgroup; it is not an intrinsic word without that context.
content.exact: For x in X, define the mirror image r·x. The object x is chiral relative to (G,H) iff r·x is not in the H-orbit H·x. Because H has index 2, the property is independent of which r in G\H is chosen.
content.example: Left and right hands are the usual physical analogy: a mirror swaps handedness, while rotations alone do not.
content.plain: A chiral object has a handedness: mirroring changes it in a way that allowed orientation-preserving motions cannot undo.

assumptions.text: A formal system S and a set Gamma of admitted premises are fixed.

content.caveat: Derivability is not identical to semantic truth. Soundness/completeness results relate the two only under stated hypotheses.
content.exact: Gamma |-_{S} P means that there exists a finite S-valid derivation whose undischarged premises are permitted by Gamma and whose final formula is P.
content.example: Whether a statement is derivable can change when axioms or inference rules change.
content.plain: Writing Gamma |- P means that P can be reached by a finite sequence of allowed proof steps from the declared axioms and premises.

content.exact: For a set X, a relation ~ on X is an equivalence relation iff (i) for every x in X, x~x; (ii) for all x,y in X, x~y implies y~x; and (iii) for all x,y,z in X, x~y and y~z imply x~z.
content.example: Congruence modulo 2 partitions the integers into the even and odd equivalence classes.
content.plain: A relation is an equivalence relation when it behaves like equality with respect to reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity.

content.caveat: The existence and uniqueness of halves depend on the ambient algebraic structure.
content.exact: Given a structure with an addition operation, y is a half of x when y+y=x. A unique halving operation x↦x/2 exists only in contexts where this equation has exactly one solution y for each x under consideration.
content.example: In the real numbers, half of 7 is 7/2. In the integers, 7 has no integer half. In arithmetic modulo 5, 2 has a unique multiplicative inverse 3, so division by 2 is well-defined.
content.plain: “Half of x” is not one universal operation. It depends on what x is and which operations exist in its mathematical structure.

content.example: 18 is even because 18=2·9. 19 is odd because 19=2·9+1.
content.plain: Every integer belongs to one of two classes: even or odd.

content.caveat: This seed record uses the standard positive-integer definition; “prime elements” in general rings require separate contextual definitions.
content.exact: For p in Z with p>1, p is prime iff for every positive integer d, d divides p implies d=1 or d=p.
content.example: 7 is prime. 12 is not prime because 3 divides 12 and 3 is neither 1 nor 12.
content.plain: A prime cannot be factored into two smaller positive integers greater than 1.

assumptions.text: F:T^k→X is periodic in each angular coordinate, where T=R/(2πZ).
ω in R^k is a frequency vector.

content.caveat: “Quasiperiodic” has other precise meanings in tilings, symbolic dynamics, cocycles, and other areas. Each use must state its convention.
content.exact: Under this convention, f:R->X has a quasiperiodic torus representation when f(t)=F(theta_0+omega t), where F:T^k->X, theta_0 in T^k, and omega in R^k. A commonly imposed nonresonance condition is rational independence of the components of omega: m·omega=0 for m in Z^k implies m=0. Nonperiodicity of f does not follow from that condition alone if F has additional symmetries or degeneracies.
content.example: f(t)=cos(t)+cos(sqrt(2)t) is nonperiodic and has a two-frequency quasiperiodic representation under this convention.
content.plain: A common quasiperiodic model combines several angular motions whose basic frequencies are rationally independent. The representation itself must be distinguished from the extra conditions needed to guarantee that the resulting function is nonperiodic.

content.caveat: Sensitivity alone is not a universal definition of chaos.
content.exact: T has sensitive dependence on initial conditions iff there exists δ>0 such that for every x in X and every ε>0 there exist y in X and n>=0 with d(x,y)<ε and d(T^n(x),T^n(y))>δ.
content.example: In chaotic systems, small initial discrepancies may become macroscopically separated under iteration.
content.plain: Sensitivity formalizes one kind of error amplification: no matter how closely two starting states are chosen, some nearby state can eventually move a definite distance away.
